extracted.intended_audience: Harvard SEAS researchers, faculty, and staff preparing press releases / research communications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating short (600–800 word) press releases about research or institutional news aimed at non-technical readers and media outlets; includes criteria to decide whether a release is warranted and coordination considerations for collaborative work or journal embargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases, typically 600–800 word summaries written for a non-technical reader, are distributed to members of the media (and others) to highlight a newsworthy activity, event, or major institutional change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the release concise (about 600–800 words) and write for a non-technical reader; frame the piece as a short summary meant to attract media attention rather than as a technical paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major scientific implications or practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the research have major scientific implications or practical applications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A press release is more likely to be warranted if the work meaningfully advances understanding or has clear, significant real-world uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: News hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a news hook (i.e., something broad-based that a reporter might find intriguing)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify an angle or element that makes the story immediately interesting to a general audience or a reporter; without a good hook, media uptake will be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groundbreaking, original, and timely
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the research groundbreaking, original, and timely?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize novelty and timeliness; routine incremental results or work that lacks novelty are less likely to justify a release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual or unexpected findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the research unusual or unexpected (e.g., how a Venus flytrap snaps or creating bubbles that maintain their shape for a year)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising or counterintuitive results tend to attract media interest—use concrete, evocative examples when describing the unexpected aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of engaging visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you have engaging or beautiful accompanying photos, movies, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality visuals (photos, videos, graphics) increase the appeal and shareability of a release; include or arrange such assets when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property / industry partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a patent pending or collaboration with industry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents or industry collaborations can increase newsworthiness and may require coordination with partners and legal/technology transfer offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of awards
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major, widely recognized awards generally justify their own press releases; less prominent awards may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal publication and embargo policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work is being published in a journal, what is the embargo policy? Does the journal issue its own press releases or promote authors in other ways?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the journal's embargo rules and promotional activities before issuing a release; coordinate timing to respect embargoes and avoid duplication or conflicts with journal communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination for collaborative work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work is collaborative, have you discussed the possibility of issuing a press release with your colleagues? (In such cases, it is wise to have the SEAS Communications Office coordinate efforts with other institutions and organizations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-institutional or multi-author projects, discuss release plans early and coordinate messaging, timing, and responsibilities—ideally via the central communications office to ensure consistent outreach.
